interactions: Warfarin + ibuprofen: major interaction; platelet COX-1 inhibition and gastrointestinal mucosal injury add to the anticoagulant effect, and protein-binding displacement can transiently raise free warfarin; the INR change is variable; bleeding risk is markedly increased
Ibuprofen + lisinopril: NSAIDs blunt prostaglandin-dependent renal perfusion and the antihypertensive effect; acute kidney injury risk, higher in the elderly and with volume depletion

Warfarin + fosphenytoin or phenytoin: phenytoin may transiently raise the INR at the start and then lowers it by enzyme induction; warfarin can raise phenytoin levels; frequent INR and phenytoin level monitoring
Warfarin + valproate: protein-binding displacement raises free warfarin, and valproate impairs platelet function and can lower platelet counts; additive bleeding risk
Warfarin + carbamazepine: CYP induction lowers the warfarin effect within days to weeks
Warfarin + levetiracetam: no clinically significant interaction
Donepezil + fosphenytoin or phenytoin: additive bradycardia risk during IV loading; phenytoin induction can lower donepezil levels
output.proposed: Warfarin, ibuprofen, lisinopril and donepezil (current) against antiseizure options (levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine)
output.summary: NSAID with warfarin is a major bleeding interaction, and NSAID with an ACE inhibitor impairs renal perfusion. Among antiseizure drugs, phenytoin, valproate and carbamazepine interact with warfarin; levetiracetam does not.

results.key_finding: For vitamin K antagonist-associated intracranial hemorrhage with an INR of 1.4 or more, IV vitamin K 10 mg and a prothrombin complex concentrate are recommended over fresh frozen plasma, with a repeat INR after administration.
results.title: Guideline for reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial hemorrhage

output.summary: Warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage is reversed with IV vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate rather than plasma [Frontera_2016]. Whether and when to resume anticoagulation after a subdural hematoma rests on observational data and weighs thromboembolic risk against recurrence; strictly lobar microhemorrhages raise the risk of recurrent intracranial bleeding. Focal status epilepticus is treated with the staged protocol under continuous EEG [Brophy_2012].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform an LP: a subdural hematoma with 8 mm midline shift and uncal herniation, and an INR of 4.8, contraindicate it.
Do not continue or restart warfarin before the hemorrhage is treated and the decision is reviewed.
Do not proceed to surgery before INR reversal to below 1.4 [Frontera_2016].
Do not use fresh frozen plasma as the reversal agent when PCC is available [Frontera_2016].
Do not continue ibuprofen or any other NSAID.
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016].
Reverse warfarin now: IV vitamin K 10 mg plus 4-factor PCC (35 units/kg for an INR of 4 to 6, maximum 3500 units), with a repeat INR after the infusion and a target below 1.4 [Frontera_2016].

Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), maintenance adjusted to creatinine clearance, and avoid fosphenytoin and valproate because both interact with warfarin and valproate impairs platelet function in an active hemorrhage [ESETT_2019].
Urgent neurosurgical evacuation of the acute-on-chronic SDH (12 mm, 8 mm midline shift, early uncal herniation) once the INR is corrected.
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].
Hold warfarin and stop ibuprofen; use acetaminophen for pain; hold lisinopril while creatinine is raised.
Treat the urinary tract infection with IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily after the urine culture, adjusted to susceptibility.
Decide on resuming anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation only after evacuation, weighing thromboembolic risk against recurrence and the lobar microhemorrhages.

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography does not change acute management of a subdural hematoma with NCSE in known atrial fibrillation.
Atrial fibrillation is known and seen on standard ICU monitoring; Holter adds nothing to acute management.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.
LP is contraindicated with a 12 mm SDH, 8 mm midline shift and an INR of 4.8: herniation and bleeding risk, and no indication when the SDH explains the presentation.

patient.history_present_illness: A 77-year-old White female retired librarian was brought to the emergency department by her son after she was found increasingly difficult to rouse this morning. Her son reports she lives alone and had called him last night complaining of a headache and feeling 'fuzzy-headed.' When he arrived this morning, she was in bed, and he witnessed what he described as generalized stiffening and rhythmic jerking of her arms and legs lasting approximately 2 minutes. After the shaking stopped, she was still not back to normal. He called 911. On EMS assessment, 30 minutes after the observed seizure, she was awake but staring blankly, answering only 'yes' or 'no,' with significant word-finding difficulty. She has a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and moderate Alzheimer's dementia. She lives alone with daily check-ins from her son. Her baseline per son is that she is oriented to her name and sometimes the year, speaks in short sentences, needs help with medications, but is independent with basic ADLs. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, donepezil, and lisinopril. Her son reports her INR was therapeutic at her last check 3 weeks ago (2.4). However, she has been taking several doses of over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain for the past 10 days. She has no prior history of seizures. No recent falls per son. Temperature at scene 38.0°C per EMS. Urine was foul-smelling per son who changed her pad this morning. Son suspects urinary tract infection.
